title: On the Convergence of Stochastic Low-Rank Adaptation
abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) optimizes $J(B,A)=\mathcal L(W_\mathrm{base}+sBA)$ over two adapters $B \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times r}$ and $A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times n}$ that form a low-rank update to a frozen pretrained weight matrix $W_\mathrm{base} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$. The prior analysis shows LoRA-GD takes $\exp\{\mathcal{O}(ε^{-2})\}$ oracle calls to find an $ε$-stationary point such that $\|\nabla J(B,A)\|\leq ε$ in the deterministic setting. We sharpen the analysis and show that $\mathcal{O}(ε^{-4})$ full-gradient evaluations suffice for the same first-order criterion. We further study stochastic LoRA under unbiased gradient estimates and finite variance. We propose LoRA-NSGDM, which finds an $ε$-stationary point with $\mathcal{O}(ε^{-8})$ stochastic oracle complexity. Under the additional mean-square smoothness condition, we use variance reduction strategy and propose LoRA-STORM, which improves the stochastic oracle complexity to $\mathcal{O}(ε^{-6})$.

Under the additional mean-square smoothness condition, we use variance reduction strategy and propose LoRA-STORM, which improves the stochastic oracle complexity to 𝒪 ​ ( ϵ − 6 ) \mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-6}) . 1 Introduction Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) freezes a pretrained weight matrix W base ∈ ℝ m × n W_{\mathrm{base}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m	imes n} and parameterizes the adapted matrix W ∈ ℝ m × n W\in\mathbb{R}^{m	imes n} as W = W base + s ​ B ​ A W=W_{\mathrm{base}}+sBA , where s > 0 s>0 is a fixed scaling factor, B ∈ ℝ m × r B\in\mathbb{R}^{m	imes r} , and A ∈ ℝ r × n A\in\mathbb{R}^{r	imes n} , with typically r ≪ min ⁡ { m , n } r\ll\min\{m,n\} . Thus, B ​ A BA is the trainable low-rank update (Hu et al. , 2022 ) . Writing F ​ ( X ) := ℒ ​ ( W base + s ​ X ) F(X):=\mathcal{L}(W_{\mathrm{base}}+sX) , LoRA solves min B , A ⁡ J ​ ( B , A ) := F ​ ( B ​ A ) . \min_{B,A}J(B,A):=F(BA). This parameterization substantially reduces the number of trainable parameters and the optimizer-state memory, making LoRA a standard tool for adapting large models, including in privacy-preserving federated and decentralized fine-tuning (Sun et al. , 2024 ; Ghiasvand et al. , 2025 ) . The motivation for LoRA is consistent with earlier evidence that pretrained language models can be fine-tuned effectively in low-dimensional parameter subspaces (Aghajanyan et al. , 2021 ) . Subsequent variants extend LoRA in complementary directions: QLoRA combines low-rank adaptation with a quantized frozen model (Dettmers et al. , 2023 ) ; LoRA+ uses factor-specific learning rates (Hayou et al. , 2024 ) ; PiSSA initializes the factors from principal singular components of the pretrained weight (Meng et al. , 2024 ) ; and LoRA-GA uses the initial full-fine-tuning gradient to choose the factor initialization (Wang et al. , 2024 ) . Empirical comparisons further show that similar downstream accuracy does not make LoRA equivalent to full fine-tuning: the two methods can differ in what they learn and forget and in the spectral structure of their weight updates (Biderman et al. , 2024 ; Shuttleworth et al. , 2025 ) . Despite its practical success, even the simple simultaneous two-factor LoRA-GD update is challenging to analyze. As observed in prior work (Sun et al. , 2024 ; Malinovsky et al. , 2024 ) , even when F F has a Lipschitz gradient, the factored objective J ​ ( B , A ) = F ​ ( B ​ A ) J(B,A)=F(BA) generally has no globally Lipschitz gradient in ( B , A ) (B,A) because the map ( B , A ) ↦ B ​ A (B,A)\mapsto BA is bilinear. Thus standard smooth nonconvex convergence theory does not directly apply to the simultaneous factor dynamics. Existing theory addresses several complementary questions. It characterizes LoRA’s expressive power (Zeng and Lee, 2024 ) , its landscape in the NTK and more general regimes (Jang et al. , 2024 ; Kim et al. , 2025 ) , and continuous-time dynamics for matrix factorization (Xu et al. , 2025 ) . Other analyses rely on infinite-width limits or modify the factor update through unequal learning rates, preconditioning, or structured factors (Hayou et al. , 2024 ; Zhang and Pilanci, 2024 ; Ding et al. , 2026 ) . These results do not provide a finite-time stationarity guarantee for the original simultaneous two-factor LoRA-GD update on a general smooth nonconvex loss. Recently, Mu and Klabjan ( 2026 ) provides a non-asymptotic analysis of LoRA-GD under smoothness and lower boundedness of F F . They prove that LoRA-GD converges at a rate of min 0 ≤ t < T ⁡ ‖ ∇ J ​ ( B t , A t ) ‖ F 2 = 𝒪 ​ ( 1 log ⁡ T ) . \min_{0\leq t<T}\left\|
abla J(B_{t},A_{t})ight\|_{F}^{2}=\mathcal{O}\!\left( rac{1}{\log T}ight). This rate yields an exponential complexity bound exp ⁡ { 𝒪 ​ ( ϵ − 2 ) } \exp\{\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2})\} for finding an ϵ \epsilon -stationary point, which is not satisfactory. This motivates us to ask Q1. Can we improve the iteration complexity of LoRA-GD to a polynomial bound? Despite the non-asymptotic analysis for the deterministic setting, the stochastic counterpart remains open in Mu and Klabjan ( 2026 ) , which identifies the control of a fourth-order noise moment as a central difficulty. Existing stochastic guarantees either impose additional global regularity and trajectory conditions (Jiang et al. , 2024 ) or alter the factor update (Sokolov et al. , 2025 ) . Neither establishes convergence of simultaneous stochastic LoRA under finite variance alone. This motivates our second question: Q2. Can a simultaneous stochastic LoRA method be proved convergent under standard finite variance assumptions? We answer both questions affirmatively through the following contributions. • In the deterministic setting, we sharpen the trajectory analysis of Mu and Klabjan ( 2026 ) and prove that 𝒪 ​ ( ϵ − 4 ) \mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-4}) full-gradient evaluations suffice to find ( B , A ) (B,A) satisfying ‖ ∇ J ​ ( B , A ) ‖ F ≤ ϵ \left\|

We prove that LoRA-NSGDM returns random factors ( B , A ) (B,A) satisfying 𝔼 ​ ‖ ∇ J ​ ( B , A ) ‖ F ≤ ϵ \mathbb{E}\left\|

In particular, we compare the convergence of LoRA-NSGDM and LoRA-STORM with LoRA-GD using the adaptive stepsizes of Mu and Klabjan ( 2026 ) . We consider three tasks. The first trains logistic regression on pretrained image representations on CIFAR-10. The second trains a LoRA-parameterized ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10. The third fine-tunes TinyLlama-1.1B on Alpaca. We evaluate LoRA-STORM only in the logistic-regression experiment. Although LoRA-STORM offers improved stochastic-oracle complexity in theory, each iteration requires two stochastic-oracle evaluations. This additional cost makes LoRA-STORM less attractive for the larger-scale ResNet-18 and TinyLlama experiments, where we compare LoRA-NSGDM with the LoRA-GD baselines. Unless stated otherwise, we follow the experimental protocol of Mu and Klabjan ( 2026 ) , which includes the datasets, architectures, LoRA ranks, factor initializations, batch sizes, and training horizons. The baselines are LoRA-GD with their η adapt \eta^{\mathrm{adapt}} , η adapt2 \eta^{\mathrm{adapt2}} , and η norm \eta^{\mathrm{norm}} stepsizes. Following Mu and Klabjan ( 2026 ) , we omit η adapt \eta^{\mathrm{adapt}} from the ResNet-18 and TinyLlama experiments because computing the required gradient with respect to the matrix B ​ A BA incurs substantial memory overhead for large models. Within each experiment, all methods use the same data split, initial predictor, and minibatch order. Appendix F gives the complete experimental settings and hyperparameters. 6.1 Logistic regression Figure 1: Training a rank-4 LoRA logistic-regression classifier on CIFAR-10 representations. We consider logistic regression on CIFAR-10 representations extracted by an ImageNet-pretrained Deng et al. ( 2009 ) ResNet-18 model He et al. ( 2016 ) . Figure 1 presents the convergence comparison. Each CIFAR-10 image is passed once through the pretrained network. We use the resulting 512-dimensional penultimate-layer representation as the input to the linear classifier. These representations are computed before training and are shared by all methods. The classifier weight is W 0 + B ​ A W_{0}+BA . The base matrix W 0 W_{0} is fixed, and only the rank-4 factors A A and B B are trained. We initialize A A with PyTorch’s Kaiming-uniform rule, and set B = 0 B=0 . Training uses cross-entropy, shuffled minibatches of size 512, no weight decay, and 88 steps per epoch. Panels (a) and (b) of Figure 1 show the first 60 epochs. In Figure 1 a and 1 b, LoRA-NSGDM exhibits faster convergence than the LoRA-GD algorithms. Over the final 2,000 updates shown in Figure 1 (b), LoRA-STORM attains the lowest mean loss. 6.2 ResNet-18 training Figure 2: Training ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10 with rank-20 LoRA. We train a ResNet-18 directly on CIFAR-10. Rank-20 LoRA factors are applied to the convolution layers. The output layer is trained without a rank constraint. Batch normalization layers are disabled following the settings in Mu and Klabjan ( 2026 ) . We use minibatches of size 512, cross-entropy, and no weight decay. Each method is trained for 22,000 steps. Figure 2 shows the results over the first 250 epochs. LoRA-NSGDM converges significantly faster and more steadily than LoRA-GD algorithms. 6.3 TinyLlama-1.1B fine-tuning Figure 3: Fine-tuning TinyLlama-1.1B on Alpaca with rank-32 LoRA under (a) small-factor and (b) large-factor initialization. We evaluate the methods on TinyLlama-1.1B instruction fine-tuning. Figure 3 compares small-factor and large-factor initialization. We fine-tune TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat-v1.0 (Zhang et al. , 2024 ) on Alpaca (Taori et al. , 2023 ) . Each example contains an instruction, an optional input, and a response. Sequences are padded or truncated to 512 tokens, and padding tokens are excluded from the causal-language-model loss. We reserve 2,000 examples for validation. Each optimizer update uses one minibatch of 16 examples, with no gradient accumulation. Rank-32 LoRA factors are inserted into the query, key, value, and output projections of every attention block. The base-model weights and biases remain fixed. In both initialization regimes, we set B = 0 B=0 and sample A ∼ 𝒩 ​ ( 0 , σ 2 ) A\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}) . The small-factor initialization uses σ = 10 − 3 \sigma=10^{-3} , whereas the large-factor initialization uses σ = 1 / r = 0.03125 \sigma=1/r=0.03125 . The corresponding training horizons are 500 and 250 optimizer updates, respectively. With the small-factor initialization shown in Figure 3 (a), LoRA-NSGDM converges faster than the LoRA-GD algorithms. 7 Conclusion We established finite-time convergence guarantees for simultaneous two-factor LoRA optimization. For deterministic LoRA-GD, a refined trajectory analysis improves the previously exponential sufficient complexity to 𝒪 ​ ( ϵ − 4 ) \mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-4}) full-gradient evaluations for finding V V with ‖ ∇ J ​ ( V ) ‖ F ≤ ϵ \left\|
abla J(V)ight\|_{F}\leq\epsilon . In the stochastic setting, we showed that plain LoRA-SGD can fail under finite variance alone and introduced LoRA-NSGDM , which achieve 𝒪 ​ ( ϵ − 8 ) \mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-8}) stochastic oracle complexity for 𝔼 ​ ‖ ∇ J ​ ( V ) ‖ F ≤ ϵ \mathbb{E}\left\|
abla J(V)ight\|_{F}\leq\epsilon . When the stochastic oracle additionally satisfies mean-square smoothness, LoRA-STORM evaluates each fresh sample at two consecutive iterates and improves the stochastic oracle complexity to 𝒪 ​ ( ϵ − 6 ) \mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-6}) . Together, these results give polynomial deterministic and stochastic convergence guarantees for simultaneous LoRA factor updates under the minimal oracle assumptions. References A. Aghajanyan, S.
